speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since then, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) have undertaken another review of the Companies Act to ensure our regulatory regime continues to remain robust, relevant and in line with international norms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Several rounds of public consultation on the proposed amendments were conducted and the feedback has, where appropriate, been incorporated into the amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first set of amendments seeks to make the ownership and control of business entities more transparent and thus reduce opportunities for the misuse of corporate entities for illicit purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will help Singapore to better meet the recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: FATF is an intergovernmental body that sets global standards for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and other related threats to the integrity of the international financial system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a member of FATF, Singapore undergoes mutual evaluations by FATF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Singapore's fourth mutual evaluation last year, FATF assessed that Singapore has a strong framework for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One of these was to enhance the access of law enforcement agencies to information on the beneficial ownership of legal persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore is also a member of the Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (GF).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Amending our laws will enable us to better implement international standards on tax transparency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first pertains to registers of controllers, members and nominee directors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are requiring three new registers to be maintained by companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, clause 47 will require locally incorporated companies and foreign companies registered in Singapore to maintain registers of their controllers at prescribed places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A controller, or more commonly known as the beneficial owner, refers to an individual or a legal entity that has interest in or significant control over the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill defines "significant control" and "significant interest" and uses a 25% threshold to help companies determine when control and interest are significant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The 25% threshold is consistent with those in the FATF's guidance documents, the United Kingdom's (UK's) legislation on registers of people with significant control, and the European Union's Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Companies will be required to take reasonable steps to identify and obtain information on their controllers, including sending notices to potential controllers or persons who have information about the controllers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides companies, the Bill will introduce obligations for two other groups of persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, any person who receives a notice from the company must provide his particulars to the company if he is a controller.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the person is not the controller, the person must provide any information on the controller that he is aware of to the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, controllers will be required to provide and update their particulars to the companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Internationally, there are discussions about central or public registers of controllers and the automatic exchange of beneficial ownership information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the Group of 20 (G20), there is greater focus on ensuring availability of beneficial ownership information of legal persons to regulators and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill only requires companies to maintain non-public registers of controllers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, this information must be provided to the Registrar and law enforcement authorities upon request.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also provides a reserve power for the Minister to direct the Registrar to maintain a central register of controllers should it become necessary to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 46 will require foreign companies registered in Singapore to maintain public registers of their members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This brings the position of foreign companies into alignment with the current requirement for locally incorporated companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The change will not impose any additional compliance responsibility for foreign companies which already maintain registers of members in their place of incorporation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 47 will require locally incorporated companies to maintain the third new register, which is the register of nominee directors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill will also require nominee directors to disclose their nominee status and the particulars of their nominators to their companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This mitigates the risks of money laundering and terrorist financing being done through nominees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, record retention, or the second key change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When a company is wound up, clause 38 will require the liquidator to retain the company's records for at least five years, instead of the current two.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Furthermore, a company that is wound up by its members or creditors will not be allowed to destroy records early.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such a company will have to retain its records for at least five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For a company that has been struck off and dissolved, clause 39 will require its former officers to similarly retain all books and papers of the company for at least five years, including its accounting records and registers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The five-year period takes reference from standards under FATF and GF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The changes will allow enforcement agencies to access past records for their investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA will also issue further guidance to companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes samples of the notice that companies can use to send to their shareholders, directors and any other relevant persons to assist them in obtaining the information required for their register of controllers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These seek to reduce the regulatory burden and improve the ease of doing business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, clause 42 introduces an inward re-domiciliation regime in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Foreign corporate entities will be allowed to transfer their registration to Singapore, besides the current options of setting up a subsidiary or branch in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Inward re-domiciliation is akin to changing "corporate citizenship".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Transfer of registration will thus be useful to foreign corporate entities that wish to retain their corporate history and identity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Foreign corporate entities may choose to re-domicile for various reasons, such as for a more conducive regulatory framework or to be closer to their shareholders or operational base.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A foreign corporate entity that is re-domiciled to Singapore will be required to comply with the requirements of the Companies Act like any other Singapore company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, clauses 9 to 10 and 14 to 16 will align the timelines for holding annual general meetings (AGMs) and filing annual returns with the companies' financial year end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also exempts all private companies from holding AGMs, subject to safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will be in addition to the current regime whereby private companies can dispense with the holding of AGMs if all shareholders approve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also includes safeguards, such as allowing any shareholder of a private company to ask for an AGM within prescribed timelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, clause 6 will remove the requirement for a common seal to execute documents, such as deeds, and for certain documents, such as share certificates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The use of common seals has become outdated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Jurisdictions, such as Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, New Zealand and the United Kingdom (UK) no longer require the use of common seals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill will allow companies to execute documents by having them signed by company officers who are duly authorised to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, notwithstanding this amendment, companies can choose to retain the use of a common seal based on their business needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Debt restructuring refers to the process undertaken by companies in financial difficulty to renegotiate the terms of their debts and save their businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The need for debt restructuring is on the rise globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Recent high-profile cases include Hanjin Shipping's attempted rehabilitation in Korea and ongoing efforts for Singapore-listed businesses like Swiber and Ezra.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A successful restructuring averts liquidation and allows the company to continue as a going concern, which benefits not only the company owners but also employees who keep their jobs and others who rely on the company for their own businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It also allows the company's creditors to receive a higher repayment under the restructuring proposal than in liquidation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While Singapore is already a regional forum of choice for restructuring, these amendments will enhance Singapore's restructuring processes which are schemes of arrangement, under section 210 of the Bill, and judicial management, under Part VIIIA of the Bill; and improve our capability to deal with cross-border insolvencies and restructurings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These proposed changes will further enhance our restructuring framework and status as a centre for international debt restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With this background in mind, let me explain the key amendments relating to restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will first cover amendments to the schemes of arrangement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In a scheme, the company presents a debt restructuring proposal at meetings of its creditors or classes of them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the proposal is approved by a majority of creditors that hold 75% of the company's debts at these meetings and is sanctioned by the Court, the proposal becomes binding on the creditors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The key amendment is clause 22, which introduces a new set of provisions that apply to schemes which implement debt restructuring proposals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These provisions adapt parts of Chapter 11 of the United States (US) Bankruptcy Code (Chapter 11).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will highlight the key features of these new provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The provisions will allow the Court to order a moratorium in favour of a company that is proposing or intends to propose a scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The moratorium prevents creditors from taking action against the company, such as commencing legal proceedings or enforcing security rights, and gives the company breathing room to put forward the restructuring proposal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will address situations where the moratorium may cause disproportionately adverse effects on certain transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example is contractual obligations under set-off and netting arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The next feature of Chapter 11 that is being adapted are rescue financing provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Rescue financing consists of new loans which provide working capital during the restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Without rescue financing, a viable company may be unable to restructure, but lenders may be reluctant to provide additional financing to troubled companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That means priority over all other debts or to be secured by a security interest that has priority over pre-existing security interests, provided the pre-existing interests are adequately protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is consistent with the approach in Chapter 11.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another feature adapted from Chapter 11 is to allow the Court to approve a scheme even if there are dissenting creditor classes, but provided safeguards are met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Presently, the Court can only sanction a scheme if the requisite majority approval has been obtained from all classes of creditors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These provisions, therefore, prevent a minority dissenting classes of creditors from unreasonably frustrating a restructuring that benefits creditors as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The final feature adapted from Chapter 11 are provisions for pre-negotiated restructurings between the company and its key creditors or "pre-packs".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Other creditors will not be affected as the pre-pack is sufficient to save the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The new provisions facilitate approval of these pre-packs as the Court may dispense with calling creditor meetings if certain safeguards are met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now move on to amendments relating to our judicial management scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Judicial management is a temporary Court-supervised procedure where a company unable to pay its debts is managed by a judicial manager.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will allow the judicial management process to commence earlier in the day, when the prospects of saving a company are higher.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 25(d) will allow the Court to make a judicial management order despite objections from certain secured creditors if the prejudice caused to unsecured creditors is disproportionately greater.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Presently, the Court cannot grant a judicial management order if these secured creditors oppose the application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 28 will introduce rescue financing provisions, which mirror the provisions introduced for schemes of arrangement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These three enhancements to the judicial management regime will improve its efficacy as a corporate rescue process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now turn to amendments pertinent to cross-border cases, which are increasingly common because businesses conduct their operations and dealings all over the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 40 sets out a list of factors for the Court to consider when deciding whether a foreign company has substantial connection to Singapore in order for it to be wound up under this Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The impact of this list goes beyond winding up, as a foreign company that can be wound up under this Act may make an application for a scheme of arrangement or judicial management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This list will provide greater certainty to foreign debtors that wish to restructure in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 45 abolishes the current rule that requires liquidators of foreign companies to "ring fence" Singapore assets and pay off debts incurred in Singapore first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, "ring fencing" for specific financial entities, such as banks and insurance companies, will still be retained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These amendments will provide greater certainty of outcome in cross-border cases and significantly enhance Singapore's capability in dealing with cross-border insolvencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill will also reduce the regulatory burden on companies and improve corporate governance in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The enhanced debt restructuring framework will give business entities in financial difficulties greater flexibility to restructure and survive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Together with the new inward re-domiciliation regime, these amendments will increase our competitiveness and strengthen Singapore as a leading financial centre.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I will focus my speech on the third basket of the amendments which the Senior Minister of State has mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Where such restructuring is carried out successfully, cost efficiently and relatively quickly, all stakeholders, including creditors, investors, shareholders and employees, benefit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For companies that have fallen on hard times, but with a sound underlying business, restructuring is preferable to the alternative of liquidation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In contrast, in a liquidation, the company's assets will be broken up, sold for recovery and distributed to creditors, usually at fire sale prices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Further, in an economic downturn, our restructuring regime allows struggling companies to quickly resume normal business operations which enhances the growth and sustainability of our economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The need for Singapore to have a robust insolvency framework is underscored by the difficulties which the global economy has faced in recent times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In 2016, we witnessed increasing global uncertainty, climbing interest rates and a downturn in oil prices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Global corporate defaults were at their highest since the 2008 financial crisis, economic growth slowed and the economic outlook was severely dampened.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In the second half 2016 alone, companies like Swissco Holdings, Swiber Holdings, Technics Oil and Gas Ltd, Ezra Holdings, all major players in the beleaguered oil offshore and marine industry, went into one form of insolvency arrangement or another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The adverse run-on effects of the insolvency and collapse of a company cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not just the closure of a business, but also the loss of jobs and livelihoods for many.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The threat of the loss of jobs in this industry as well as others is thus a real issue, close to the hearts of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There are also other stakeholders whose interests we need to consider, such as financial institutions with loan exposures to distressed companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The rehabilitation of such companies in financial trouble is, therefore, not just about crunching numbers, generating business or increasing profits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is a wider social interest at stake.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is in this context and backdrop that this Bill has been introduced, and it is aimed at several key objectives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, it seeks to set up a more conducive legal framework with a view to ultimately saving businesses, preserving values and jobs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, it aims to make our insolvency and restructuring laws more robust, more rescue-friendly but, at the same time, nimble and nuanced enough to balance and protect the competing interests of relevant parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Third, I would suggest that this is also timely for the reasons the Senior Minister of State has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Since the last amendment to these regimes, the way we do business now is very different; there are a lot of cross-border aspects of the business, and many companies are located in several parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, a company may be headquartered in one country but have branches in others, and therefore, assets, interests, creditors or debtors are located across different jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There had been a slew of enhancements to the regime and, as a practitioner in this area, I can say that it has been broadly welcomed by insolvency practitioners from the finance industry, banks and the companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I wish to focus on five of those amendments which the Senior Minister of State has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, the proposed section 211B(1) widens the circumstances in which a company can obtain a moratorium when seeking such a scheme or compromise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The moratorium is crucial because it suspends actions against a debtor company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Without a moratorium, a scramble usually takes place when creditors think that someone else is going to steal a march on them and, consequently, everyone moves in to liquidate the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This undermines any prospect of being able to reach a more beneficial arrangement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It drives a company towards litigation and, ultimately, kills value in the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In contrast, a moratorium holds the line and keeps all creditors on an even keel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is vital, so that companies in distress can have some "breathing space" in order to put in place an effective and mutually beneficial rescue plan.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is necessary to give efficacy to the moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, the Bill also strikes a balance between the interests of the debtor company and its secured and unsecured creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The company is required to give information on its financial affairs to its creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Court takes all of this into account and is then empowered to grant a number of different restraining orders which can be ordered individually or in combination, as necessary or as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As such, the Court can bespoke the scope of the moratorium and its terms to fit the specific circumstances of each case and need not order a moratorium over security enforcement, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, the new cram-down provisions which the Senior Minister of State mentioned will better allow judicial control of schemes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As the Senior Minister of State outlined, the current regime requires there to be a threshold of 75% by value and 50% in number before a scheme can even be presented to Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In other words, the Court will have no jurisdiction to entertain any scheme proposal that does not even meet this threshold.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In the case of some companies, one class of creditors could have just a very few number of creditors and this could then, by way of this very minority number of creditors, derail the entire scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Commentators have said that this is a "major impediment" to the success of the scheme for distressed companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, there are safeguards to protect these rights of the objecting creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Court must be satisfied that the scheme does not discriminate unfairly among the classes and it must be fair and equitable to the dissenting class of creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Very often, a minority number of creditors hold a tactical leverage in restructurings to try to negotiate a better position for themselves, even if they hold only a small percentage of the debts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, think this change is a welcome one, which calibrates the playing field a little more in favour of the debtor company and its majority creditors, without compromising the position of other dissenting creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Third, it will now be easier for companies to apply for judicial management.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Under the current Companies Act, the Court must be satisfied that the company "is" or "will be" unable to pay its debts, before allowing the application to succeed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As noted by ILRC in 2013, this strict test causes companies to turn to judicial management only when they are already hopelessly insolvent, by which time, it would often be too far gone for a judicial manager to be effective in turning the company around.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And that perhaps explains why judicial management in Singapore has been less successful in rehabilitating companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This, in my view, is a pity, as judicial management is otherwise a very useful option in our arsenal of restructuring tools.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: A Court-appointed Judicial Manager is usually an independent professional advisor, coming in to manage the affairs of a company in a difficult period, lending assurance that the creditors to the company need.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is a lower threshold and, in my view, a far more sensible one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, rescue-financing will now be encouraged under the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: New financing is often crucial for ailing companies, as it provides funds, for example, to pay urgent operational expenses, provide working capital and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Quite understandably, however, an insolvent company in such a situation is unlikely to be flushed with options when it comes to new financing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Financial institutions will not want to risk throwing good money after bad.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As such, companies in financial distress typically face severe liquidity problems, meaning they cannot meet their current liabilities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It would be futile to put such a company into a scheme or judicial management without also having the ability to facilitate a financial solution to its liquidity problems.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The rescue finance provisions, therefore, provide an option for companies to get new funds in as part of their restructuring exercise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In this respect, the new provisions allow a variety of options with varying degrees of guarantee of recovery.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, the Court could order that the debt rank in priority or it could order that the debt be secured by a security interest that ranks higher than an existing one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, the Bill also introduces safeguards which will be scrutinised and policed by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is only allowed in appropriate circumstances and the Court must be satisfied that there is "adequate protection" given to an existing security interest holder.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This, as the Senior Minister of State mentioned, draws inspiration from the US Chapter 11 model.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The rationale for the above safeguard was that new lending should create new value for the company such that it is in a position to protect the interests of the security holder, whether by cash payments or by providing another form of security.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In this way, the Courts are called upon to "assess the viability of the purpose behind the proposed financing".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Bill facilitates rescue financing for distressed companies whilst also managing any entailing risks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The US experience in Chapter 11 proceedings has been that rescue financings are invariably value enhancing and are usually associated with a higher probability of successful recovery.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that, with these amendments, the same will be seen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Model Law was designed not to make insolvency laws in different countries uniform, but to supplement existing laws.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As I previously mentioned, it is now commonplace for businesses to be cross-border.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The insolvency practitioner managing the restructuring will then have to coordinate different moving parts, grapple with foreign procedures, regulations, laws and the like.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: A degree of cooperation is thus much needed between the Courts and the insolvency practitioners from different countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is far more productive and cost-efficient for cross-border insolvencies to be coordinated from one "main" jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Currently, the provisions in the Companies Act do not assist in the facilitation of cross-border insolvencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Take the example of a company in Singapore which wants to enter into a scheme of arrangement but has subsidiaries in other jurisdictions where the real value resides.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It would be no use for the holding company to apply for a scheme and a moratorium in Singapore, only to have creditors take action against his other assets located in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: When recognition is granted, the Court then has a range of options from which to grant relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, a scheme manager in Singapore can go to a jurisdiction which has adopted the Model Law for assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, he can go to a foreign court to ask for a moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In October 2016, the Singapore Judiciary hosted the first Judicial Insolvency Network conference.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This led to guidelines for the communication, coordination and cooperation in cross-border insolvencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore, Delaware and New York have already signed up to it, with Australia, England and Wales expected to follow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These are major restructuring jurisdictions, and the ability to hold joint-hearings, such as by video conference, with the objective of increasing cooperation, aligning positions and cutting costs, can only benefit the insolvent company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: London and New York have long been regarded as the dominant force in this area.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, Madam, can the Members not have more time to consider such Bills properly before it is put up for Second Reading?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are various amendments relating to corporate secretarial and filing requirements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am agreeable to these proposals as they aim to improve practices and reduce regulatory burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the amendments involves the dispensation of compulsory AGMs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this issue, may I ask the Senior Minister of State whether ACRA does provide for public access suitable literature or other resources on minority rights?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, will the Government consider doing so in light of the proposed changes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe this will be useful to some shareholders as they grapple with the changes in the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, would the Government look into the possibility of streamlining the filing obligations of companies such that the annual ACRA filings can be combined with the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) tax filing into a composite submission?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe this will make compliance easier and businesses do not need to grapple with different deadlines and different filing obligations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the intention of allowing foreign companies to re-domicile as a Singapore company if this may help to attract existing foreign companies to relocate their operations and headquarters to Singapore and bring more business and investments to Singapore or enhance Singapore as a key corporate hub and business centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we may not, by these provisions, end up encouraging corporate inversion without bringing real gains to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the companies suffer reputational damage in their home countries for reasons of tax avoidance?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will Singapore, by encouraging corporate inversions, draw the ire of other countries?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will we, for example, go the way of, say, Ireland and draw the ire of countries like the US?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years ago, Australian companies BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto were under the spotlight from the Australian tax authorities for what was described as the "Singapore Sling" tax avoidance scheme where they were said to have channeled profits through marketing hubs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Australian tax authorities seemed to have accepted that they were for legitimate business activities and they were under legitimate tax avoidance schemes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, it appears from media reports that our so-called "Singapore Sling" schemes were not as welcoming to the Australian taxmen as the real McCoy usually served to Aussie tourists in the Long Bar at Raffles Hotel.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I recognise that: (a) it is our sovereign right to decide freely on how we want to tax and the rules therefor; and (b) that we need to always make our tax regime attractive in many ways to attract companies to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, as a country, how we organise our tax regime must also be welcomed by other countries within the international tax environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, and as we have certainly seen after the Panama Papers episode, popular opinion around the world on the issues of tax avoidance practices has started to change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tax avoidance practices, which used to be carried out without any questions asked, together with the reputation of certain once popular offshore tax havens, have taken a beating.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure the Government has considered these issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, these are my concerns and I hope the Senior Minister of State can provide some assurances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I move on to debt restructuring and judicial management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part of the major changes to this Bill consists of various new provisions relating to debt restructuring proposals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Among other things, new features for schemes of arrangements include enhanced moratoriums against creditor action.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court will also be allowed to approve rescue financing provided for debt restructuring and to give such financing super priority over existing creditors' claims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Schemes of arrangement can also be approved even if some creditors object.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill is also making it easier for companies to apply for judicial management and there are also provisions for super priority for rescue financing in judicial management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that such priority for rescue financing, together with cram-down provisions, are concepts which are borrowed from US bankruptcy law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill will also make judicial management available to foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 1 September 2016, the Korean shipping conglomerate, Hanjin, obtained a rehabilitation order from the South Korean courts to protect itself from creditors and to allow it to restructure its debts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 17 February 2017, after five-and-a-half months, we read from media reports that the Seoul Central District Court had declared Hanjin bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After the rehabilitation order, we read in media reports of their ships being turned away by container terminals, ships abandoned without sufficient funds for operation or to pay its crew, desperate cargo owners trying hard to retrieve their cargo still stuck in containers onboard the Hanjin ships.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the insolvency declared last month, I wonder whether Hanjin or any of its creditors have really benefited from the initial order for protection.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What did the initial order for insolvency protection do for all its creditors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, many Singapore companies on the brink of insolvency often apply to the Singapore High Court for some variants of "insolvency protection" measures whose stated aims usually include restructuring business or restructuring debt payments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These may be in the form of schemes of arrangements, restructuring their debt obligations and payments, or by way of judicial management, giving a chance to rehabilitate themselves with the hope of being restored.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these schemes or measures have worked in some cases but, quite often, these schemes did not work to revive and sustain the ailing companies and eventually the companies had to be wound up.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At best, it may buy some time before a company or its key and usually secured creditors work desperately to see if they can avoid writing off the huge amount of securitised loan granted to the ailing company or its vessels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meantime, by applying for judicial management or scheme of arrangement, it stalls the efforts of other creditors who may otherwise have different recourse to pursue their debts, whether in the same jurisdiction or even abroad.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These trade creditors may have already commenced actions in court, even obtained judgment or, through admiralty claims, have arrested ships in Singapore or elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the judicial management and scheme of arrangements applications, the company would have also applied for stay of such proceedings effectively, making these proceedings ineffective.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The regime now will allow debtors to buy some time before they go.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These provisions have often been used to the advantage of troubled companies as well as their banks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That said, I hope that in the application of these laws, the Courts will not allow the balance to be shifted too far away with the interest of unsecured trade creditors in favour of ailing companies and their secured creditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Courts, as the gatekeeper, will continue to vigorously scrutinise the viability of all schemes, proposals and applications put forward by ailing companies in their application to the Courts and the applicants can be called to account for the viability of their proposals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is often the case even though many ailing companies would usually have much time to sort out their problems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Courts should require more time to scrutinise the viability of proposals made, then that should override any arguments of urgency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, all creditors should be given sufficient time to scrutinise all such applications before an order is granted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my view, in fairness to all creditors and in the interest of resolving their debt situation, ailing companies should be encouraged to consider any application for debt restructuring or judicial management a little earlier than it is usually being done now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And with the new provisions, certainly in judicial management, I hope this will definitely be done now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I next move to the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a globalised world, many companies and businesses operate globally and when somebody's company runs into problems, insolvency issues may also turn cross-border.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With businesses and assets in multiple countries, this is unavoidable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When rules of insolvency may vary from country to country, it may bring complications to insolvency procedures or proceedings with companies with businesses, assets and debts in multiple jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another reason to support this will be the fact that Singapore is a key legal hub in the world and, with an increasing number of international corporate players having a base here and doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to how Singapore adopted the Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration due to globalisation and commercial realities, the need to adopt the Model Law on cross-border insolvency arose out of similar circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as how Singapore made it easy for anyone in the world to start a business in Singapore, it is imperative to make it easier to restructure businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, a harmonisation of relevant rules and a universalist approach to insolvency should be employed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, the abolishment should assist in Singapore's ambition to become a debt restructuring hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Local creditors should also not be overly worried that this amendment gives them no protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I note that a long list of financial institutions could still receive some protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, some creditors may rely on Articles 6, 21 and 22 of the Model Law to ensure that their interests are protected under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This move allows Singapore to remain competitive, facilitate the relocation of companies to Singapore, and keep pace with other jurisdictions that have embraced this re-domiciliation mechanism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, can the Minister clarify if re-domiciled companies could represent to counterparties and the public that they are Singapore-incorporated companies upon issuance of the Notice of Transfer, or could they make only such representations after ACRA is satisfied with the submission of documents evidencing de-registration in its prior place of incorporation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also note that we will introduce how a financial year is to be calculated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a required addition in view of the fact that lodging of a company's annual returns is to be done within a prescribed period after the end of its financial year, instead of the AGM under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify under what conditions will a company's application be approved?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the retention of books and papers after a company has been struck off, may I clarify why the period is five years when a person may, within six years, after the name of the company has been struck off, apply to the Court to restore the struck off company to the Register?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, on foreign entities hoping to register in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I note that the Ministry is retaining the 60-day period for newly-registered companies to prepare all share or debenture certificates, there should also be an option for an extra 30 days − in cases where companies have more elaborate tools of debt which require in-depth legal support in their countries of origin.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This option will enhance the attractiveness of our regulatory regime for companies planning to register a new entity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can all agree that this Bill would serve to bring about significant changes to our corporate insolvency regime, which will strengthen Singapore's role in debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This could not come at a more opportune time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, companies in the maritime and oil and gas industries have a tough time due to the decline in oil prices from two years ago.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While oil prices are creeping up, a bit slowly, several Singapore Stock Exchange (SGX)-listed oil and gas companies have already gone into insolvency proceedings or are facing impending insolvency petitions from creditors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, small and medium enterprises in Singapore are coping with economic challenges to maintain their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: More private funding sources would be required to make capital expenditure in order for them to improve their business models and expand their businesses beyond Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) Report proposes creating more favourable conditions to attract venture capital and private equity firms to set up shop in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The legal community whom I spoke to found this revised Companies Bill timely and appropriate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They are also appreciative of MinLaw's consultative approach in the revision of the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Cram-down provisions were introduced to prevent creditors from undermining a scheme of arrangement when introduced.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The introduction of cram-down provisions is important to facilitate the timely rescue of a company in financial distress where time is of the essence and a long-drawn out process to resolve differences will not be in the best interests of keeping the company as a going concern.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having the Court to decide on whether a cram-down provision is to be applied against dissenting creditors to a scheme of arrangement who are not being unfairly and inequitably treated in the proposed scheme would be ideal and there is no lack of jurisprudence in the US on this and, certainly, the case law there would help form our jurisprudence in this area in time to come.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These provisions would prevent de facto shareholder veto in schemes involving debt-equity swaps where shareholder approval is required.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Such provisions would encourage experienced international distressed financiers with the experience and know-how in nursing companies back to health to invest due to potential upside they can enjoy with debt-equity swaps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that MinLaw considered this proposal but was not in favour of it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But let me give an example how this could help.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Let us consider a hypothetical situation of a company with a good track record of commercial excellence that, as a result, experiences a strong brand equity in the market.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And let us say that this company falls in bad times and experienced cash flow issues and was eventually placed under judicial management.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The company has many good ongoing prospects from across the region from which the company could continue as an ongoing concern.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are private equity investors who are interested to provide rescue funding to this company but would demand for debt-equity swap provisions in their rescue financing arrangements so as to enjoy the upside on the company's revitalisation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, due to the unwillingness of some existing shareholders with sufficient voting rights who will veto this shareholder approval for the debt-equity share swaps, the rescue financers could not get the deal they are looking at and thus dropped out of the rescue financing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Without equity participation, rescue financing would simply be less attractive and rescue financers will not be incentivised to provide the expertise in such rescue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This example that I illustrated will, hopefully, show it might be worthwhile for MinLaw to study how shareholder cram-down provisions could be advantageous to attracting experienced distressed asset investors who bring their expertise in corporate governance, corporate restructuring and distressed company management who would often want to enjoy the upside from equity participation should such rescues be successfully executed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These measures, once implemented, will have the effect of strengthening Singapore's insolvency framework and enhance Singapore's standing as an international centre for debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome these timely changes to the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Besides these amendments, other amendments address key findings in the FATF's 4th mutual evaluation of Singapore's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The FATF Mutual Evaluation Report highlighted that companies in Singapore, including foreign companies registered in Singapore, are vulnerable to criminal misuse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The FATF Report also noted that the Commercial Affairs Department has observed that there has been an increase in the number of money laundering cases involving shell companies established by non-residents based overseas since 2012.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The identification of controllers and nominee directors of companies increases transparency and facilitates investigation of serious economic crimes committed by the individuals associated with such companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Greater scrutiny would have a deterrent effect on companies and their officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will focus on the proposed FATF-related amendments to the Companies Act and comment on three areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is likely to raise corporate administrative and compliance costs for such companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While this initiative is welcome in playing our part in the global fight against financial crime, I note that there are a number of major countries which have not at this stage implemented a register of controllers of companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, the US, Canada and Australia, which have been rated by FATF between 2015 and 2016 as being partially compliant or non-compliant with the FATF recommendations of transparency and beneficial ownership of legal persons and legal arrangements in their mutual evaluation reports, do not yet have an equivalent register.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Australia is in the midst of consulting on this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Amongst the major financial centres, only the UK has, since last year, implemented a Register of Persons of Significant Control.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hong Kong is currently looking at requiring firms incorporated in the city to disclose their beneficial ownership by 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a different but similar context in 2014 relating to Singapore's intention to adopt the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) pact to swap tax information aimed at ending offshore tax evasion, our then Finance Minister Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam highlighted that Singapore would adopt the standard as long as rival wealth management centres do the same.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister explained that there must be a level playing field to minimise regulatory arbitrage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Similarly, in the present context, given that the implementation of a register would increase administrative compliance costs for companies operating in Singapore, should we consider putting this provision into effect only when there is a level playing field when the major financial centres also implement their equivalent?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This means that where the officer, employee or agent had a particular state of mind when engaging in conduct within the scope of his or her actual or apparent authority, this would be evidence that the corporation had that state of mind for the purpose of any criminal proceedings against the company for an offence, such as the company's failure to send notices to the persons whom the company knows or has reasonable grounds to believe, knows the identity of its registrable controller, or the company's failure to send notices to a controller if it knows or has reasonable grounds to believe that the particulars of the controller have changed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such legal attribution is necessary as companies may only act through natural persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the proposed amendment adopts a standard of attribution which is lower than and a departure from the existing legal standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the existing standards, to establish corporate criminal liability, the mental element of an offence must be attributed to "the directing mind and will of the corporation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The "directing mind and will of the corporation" usually refers to superior officers who carry out management functions, and not any officer, employee or agent of the company.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This threshold is not easy to meet, especially where larger companies are involved, and it is often difficult for prosecutors to prove that the "directing mind and will" of the company had knowledge of the criminal conduct to pin liability on the company.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I quote the then Attorney-General Mr Steven Chong, Senior Counsel, speaking at his Keynote Address at the Cambridge Symposium for Economic Crime in 2012, "In today's financial industry, most large organisations have hierarchies which are quite complicated and unavoidably so, due to the specialised nature of professional expertise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, this has made it easy for top executives to feign ignorance when fraudulent behaviour is uncovered, especially since they have every incentive to state that they were unaware of wrongdoings in their organisations." The Attorney-General had gone on to suggest that a measure to counter this would be to impose legal requirements to increase disclosure requirements to facilitate the identification of the executives responsible for the misdeeds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Seen in this context, the proposed amendments to stipulate a lower standard of attributing the state of mind to the corporation to pin corporate liability is understandable and justified.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should this lower standard be of general import and apply to other financial crimes?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my Parliamentary Question to the Minister for Home Affairs last month, I asked whether the Minister would consider introducing an offence for commercial organisations that fail to prevent the commission of economic crimes by persons who act on their behalf, such as employees and contractors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister also stated that the Companies Act imposes various obligations on company directors to ensure that companies adopt good corporate governance practices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Implementing "failure to prevent" offences is yet another way to make it easier to pin liability on companies for acts of their employees and agents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the route that the UK has taken in its Bribery Act, by making corporations liable for failing to prevent bribery by associated persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The UK is now consulting on whether to expand this to other forms of financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The FATF Mutual Evaluation Report made the following findings on Singapore: "Singapore's status as both a major global financial centre and an international transport hub makes it vulnerable to becoming a transit point for illicit funds generated throughout East and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Banks and other financial institutions also play an important role in ensuring that their institutions are not used as conduits for money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, I note that the proposed framework expressly prohibits companies from disclosing or making available for inspection the register of controllers to the public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This restriction on access to this register is an anomaly, given that all other registers as they exist now, such as the register of shareholders and directors, are publicly available and may be inspected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, in the UK, the information in the register has to be filed at the UK Companies House and is available online.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The registers are also open to public inspection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the residential address and date of birth of individuals concerned will not be provided except to credit reference agencies and certain public authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Only the individual's name, month and year of birth, nationality and service address will be publicly available, together with details of the interest concerned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Applications may be made to keep all information private where there is a risk of violence or intimidation in the event that the information is public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that the issue of whether information on the register, which contains personal information, should be published and easily accessible to the public is contentious.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested introducing cram-down provisions to bind shareholders to restructuring proposals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Shareholders' cram down exists in Chapter 11, but Chapter 11 is an insolvency process that reorganises both the debt and equity of a company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By contrast, the new provisions support creditor schemes, which only bind the company's creditors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current scheme process is familiar and has worked well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, at this stage, we have improved the process by adapting elements of Chapter 11 that mesh well with our scheme framework, instead of moving to a different system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, Mr Patrick Tay had made several suggestions to protect employees' claims for unpaid salaries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think it is important to distinguish between two scenarios here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is where it is a restructuring scenario and the other where it is a liquidation scenario.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for the proposals concerning employee preferential debts in a winding up, these are related to corporate liquidation, and reforms to that process will be tackled in later phases of amendments to the insolvency framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are not pertinent to this set of amendments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to this set of amendments on restructuring, Mr Patrick Tay asked a question on whether or not you could exempt employee claims from the moratorium.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I think that would defeat the purpose of a moratorium.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: See, with restructuring, what you are really trying to do is: the company is in trouble, it is bleeding, it has got a problem.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You are trying to give it breathing space where it is kind of like a "time out".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the "time out" enables you, hopefully, to get in rescue financing or to see how to restructure it so that it can continue as a going concern.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If it is done well and done properly, then these employees, hopefully, will be able to get their salaries and continue to hold on to their jobs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The difficulty of exempting them from a moratorium is that just as you are talking to somebody who is prepared to give you rescue financing, then suddenly an employee claim comes and then another group of employee claims comes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the management is trying to fight and hold off these claims as you are talking with the people who are going to put in financing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not enable the management to focus on getting the company back on its feet.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the restructuring context is slightly different and the whole idea of the moratorium is to give the company time to take stock of all the different debts and try to get it back on its feet, hopefully, for the betterment of all the creditors, including the employees, and have the employees continue in employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moving on, Mr Louis Ng queried why Article 25 of the Model Law was amended.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: States are given the flexibility to modify this Model Law and many jurisdictions have adopted the Model Law with amendments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments to Article 25 have been made to give our Courts flexibility in cooperating with foreign courts and practitioners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also in line with other jurisdictions, such as the UK.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this regard, Mr Edwin Tong has noted that the Supreme Court of Singapore has adopted the Judicial Insolvency Networks' Guidelines on Cooperation and Communication in Cross-border Insolvency Cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These guidelines are a bespoke framework which will guide our Courts on communication and coordination with other courts in cross-border insolvency matters.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Additionally, aside from Singapore, the guidelines have also been adopted by the US Bankruptcy Courts of Delaware and the Southern District of New York.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other courts are also expected to adopt these guidelines in the near future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked whether companies that have re-domiciled to Singapore under the new inward re-domiciliation regime can represent themselves as Singapore-registered companies upon issuance of the Notice of Transfer by ACRA, or only after ACRA is satisfied with the submission of documents evidencing de-registration in the company's prior place of incorporation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, if the company subsequently fails to submit documents showing its de-registration from its country of domicile, ACRA may revoke its registration in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has also suggested giving re-domiciled companies an additional 30 days, on top of the proposed 60 days, to issue share and debenture certificates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed 60-day period in the Bill is equivalent to that of public companies to issue share and debenture certificates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed period is sufficient for re-domiciled companies since the certificates will be for existing shares or debentures that are issued under the law of jurisdiction from their home jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Furthermore, the interest of the share or debenture holders in obtaining the certificates also have to be considered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked about the circumstances under which the Registrar will approve a company's application to have its first financial year longer than 18 months.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not prudent to comprehensively set these out as the reasons will vary with the unique circumstances of each company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The registrar will assess each application based on its own merits.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng's other question is on the five-year record retention period for struck-off companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The UK and Hong Kong also adopt similar periods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, Mr Pillai has asked whether the Government has considered delaying the implementation of the register of controllers until such time when there is a level playing field amongst major financial centres.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is strong and growing international momentum to increase transparency of beneficial ownership through the implementation of registers of controllers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Australia and Hong Kong are also conducting public consultation on similar reforms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also mindful of the impact of these changes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Thus, the Bill will only require companies to maintain the registers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also not gone as far as to require a central or public register of controllers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, Mr Murali Pillai has asked about the amendment on establishing the state of mind of an entity for the purposes of criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Specifically, Mr Pillai has asked why the amendment adopts the "agency principle" and not the common law position on "identification principle".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Before I address this comment, let me first provide the context of the amendment and elaborate on the "agency principle" and the "identification principle" cited by Mr Pillai.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Companies Act contains offences that apply to companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a company is a legal entity, it can only act through individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The agency and identification principles are used to determine the state of mind of a company when ascertaining whether the company committed an offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The "agency principle" states the mind of a corporation's officer, employee or agent as that of the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In contrast, the "identification principle" takes into account a narrower range of individuals, usually the senior management and company directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the register of controllers, the amendment on the state of mind of an entity uses the "agency principle".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the proposed obligations for companies, such as sending notices to potential controllers, are likely to be performed by companies' officers and employees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The provision is also a standard clause in recent Bills, such as the Info-communications Media Development Authority Act 2016, SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Act 2016, Credit Bureau Act 2016 and the Government Technology Agency Act 2016.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai has also suggested giving financial institutions access to the register of controllers to facilitate their customer due diligence processes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have considered this issue carefully as the issue was also raised during our engagement with stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There were concerns about privacy and potential misuse if the register of controllers is available for public inspections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such concerns apply even if access is limited to certain professional intermediaries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think the Member's first comment was why it was necessary to bring this Bill so quickly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He appreciated that there was a report but he had hoped for more time to consider.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, the restructuring amendments on which the Member spoke were contained in the report for the recommendations to enhance Singapore as a restructuring hub.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That report came out on 20 April 2016, and it has been in the public domain.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We went for public consultation in October and December 2016, and effectively, substantively, the provisions that we are putting in place now are the same.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is very little change from the report because the comments that we got back were really sort of finetuning comments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government gave its response on 20 February.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We brought it in at this time really because, given the current economic climate, we do not want to lose the opportunity of Singapore being a restructuring hub with these enhanced provisions as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this current environment where you can actually see that there are many companies which have a need for restructuring, we felt that it was imperative to put these amendments in place as soon as possible, so that our Courts will not lose the opportunity to hear such restructuring cases and it would also be good for our professionals, especially those in the restructuring space, because the sooner this is in place, the sooner our people will be able to get their share of the work and do the restructuring work that is very much clearly in demand out there.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked whether ACRA will provide some literature on minority rights in view of these amendments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will put the materials on its website after the Bill is passed and it will continue to engage with companies to disseminate information to the minorities who will know what their rights are.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that is an important thing to do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Dennis Tan also raised the point about inward re-domiciliation and said that he hoped that this would not incur the ire of some other countries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we abide by the arms-length principle for pricing of related party transactions and there are also mechanisms in place for the exchange of information among tax authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think the underlying principle here is that we are a substantive jurisdiction and not one of those where you can just come here purely for tax purposes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This relates to the carve-out of entities from judicial management.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The thinking for this is really to consider excluding financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there is a specialist route or track for financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our current provisions already carve out some financial institutions like banks and insurance companies.
